title: Perceptron
body:
[[Multilayer Perceptron]]

---

A single [[Neuron]] with a step activation, trained by a specific rule. Rosenblatt, 1958, and the
first thing that was recognisably machine learning: it is fitted from examples rather than
programmed.

$$
\hat y = \begin{cases} 1 & \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}
$$

The training rule is one line, and it only touches the weights when the prediction is wrong:

$$
\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \eta\,(y - \hat y)\,\mathbf{x}
$$

**The perceptron convergence theorem**: if the data is linearly separable, this terminates on a
separating hyperplane in a finite number of updates. If it is not separable, it never terminates
and never settles, which is a real failure mode, not a slow one.

## What killed it, and what that taught

A perceptron draws exactly one hyperplane, so it can only compute linearly separable functions.
`AND` and `OR` are ([[Binary Operations]]); **`XOR` is not**, and no choice of two weights and a
bias will do it. Minsky and Papert made the point in 1969 and neural-network funding collapsed for
roughly fifteen years.

The fix was already obvious in principle, stack them, but nobody had a way to train the stack:
the step function's derivative is zero everywhere it is defined, so there is no gradient to
propagate. Two changes unblocked it, and they are the same two changes that define modern
practice: **replace the step with a differentiable [[Activation Function]]** ([[Sigmoid]], later
[[ReLU]]) and **use [[Back Propagation]]** to get the gradient of a [[Loss Function]] with respect
to every weight. That gives [[Multilayer Perceptron]], which does XOR with one
[[Hidden Layer]] of two units.

## Related

- [[Multilayer Perceptron]], [[Neural Network]]: what it became
- [[Neuron]]: the same formula with the activation left general
- [[Logistic Regression]]: a perceptron with a [[Sigmoid]] instead of a step, so it outputs a
  probability and can be trained by gradient descent. The modern one-unit model
- [[Non-Linear]]: why the stack needs an activation to be worth stacking
